Senses.PreferredTarget: an injustice to the buddhas of the three times
AlternateTargets: wronging the buddhas of past, present, and future
SearchAliases: wronging the buddhas of past, present, and future
Senses.Explanation: An ‘injustice to the buddhas of the three times’ is the adverse verdict in the paired warning that explaining scripture by following its wording wrongs the buddhas, while departing from scripture by one word joins demonic speech. The uses set a double demand rather than prohibit scripture. Yezhu compares wording-bound explanation to taking an image from a mirror or fishing for the sky in water; Shanhui says one dies miserably here; Zhanran and Tian’an answer the challenge instead of supplying another explanation. Feiyin uses the warning while discussing the printing of scripture, and Baichi deliberately refuses both halves while still prescribing recitation.
Senses.Note: The formula rejects captivity to scriptural wording, not scripture itself; it must not be expanded into a general anti-text doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: The buddhas of the three times do not know it, but cats and white oxen do reverses the expected hierarchy of knowing. A lamp preserves Nanquan's saying inside Dawei's explicit quotation, after which Dawei challenges both sides of the contrast. In the stronger Ancient Venerables record, Cuiyan states the same contrast in his own hall address, raises the whisk, and says the cats and white oxen are there radiating light and shaking the earth. These are distinct uses, not parallel recensions.

Senses.Explanation: The Heaven of the Thirty-Three is the celestial realm ruled by Shakra and used in Chan hyperbole as a reachable height. The preceding instruction says that such things are ordinary fare before a monastic, who must sit in a thicket of thorns as the great site of awakening and recognize the original face amid mixing with mud and water. After asking how it can be seen, the instruction marks a raised staff and warns that even seeing it does not escape that staff. A following hall address says that, when feelings of sacred and ordinary are exhausted, true constancy stands exposed; the raised fly whisk then leaps to the Heaven of the Thirty-Three and tweaks Shakra’s nose. The image dramatizes unrestricted movement rather than literal travel advice.

Senses.Explanation: Thirty years later keeps its ordinary future-time sense while serving several kinds of distant reckoning. Yuanwu Keqin warns that his question about holding fast or letting go must not be cited incorrectly when the listener meets someone thirty years later. In the Blue Cliff Record, Yuanwu postpones his answer until this mountain monk comes out with changed bones thirty years later. The lamp account of Nanyang Huizhong uses the same interval for a forecast: with the sages remote and people lax, even finding a monk will then be difficult. An unnamed monk tells Dahui Zonggao that many people will laugh thirty years later; Dahui answers that many are laughing at him right now. These uses defer a retelling, an answer, or a consequence, while Dahui's reply rejects the proposed delay; none defines a required thirty-year discipline.

Senses.Explanation: The three-inch tongue is the speaking organ in cutting and silencing formulas, while ordinary “three inches” remains a separate measure. It is often shortened in Chan exchanges to just 'the three inches.' Baoning Renyong supplies the full form: 'I have one mouth, containing a three-inch tongue; the teeth are all complete, and there is no right and wrong it does not speak' (我有一張口，內含三寸舌。牙齒總完全，是非無不說). An unnamed questioner asks Cuiyan Lingcan to speak 'without borrowing the three inches' (不借三寸，請師道), and another unnamed questioner calls Dahui Zonggao's 'three inches' tightly guarded (老和尚三寸甚密). The omitted noun is recoverable from the explicit full form and from the predicates of speaking. The Zen bend is this use of an ordinary measure as public shorthand for the tongue, not a claim that every occurrence of three inches names speech.

Senses.Note: The fishing construction is not reassigned to the tongue merely because speech follows it. Conversely, face-skin and breath supply their own measured nouns and do not create new bare-headword meanings. The separately retained tongue sense is supported by genuine noun omission in bare public-interview uses.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense names three inches, not the three-inch tongue. Three inches is a measure whose object and dimension are supplied by its construction. In the Boatman's case, Chuanzi Decheng says, 'the line hangs a thousand feet, its intent in the deep pool; three inches from the hook, why do you not speak?' (垂絲千尺，意在深潭，離鉤三寸，子何不道). Zhang Shangying's verse preserves the same distance from the hook. Fozhao Deguang uses the measure for thickness when he says Huangbo's facial skin remains three inches thick (面皮厚三寸). Tianru Weize's mortality warning applies the same small-span image to breath: 'when the three-inch breath is cut off, one fire burns through' (三寸氣斷，一火洞然). Distance, thickness, and the measured-breath image differ in what is measured, not in the lexical value of three inches; they therefore remain one sense rather than three context-driven senses.

Senses.Note: One referent covers both breath ending and breath prolonged.

Senses.Explanation: Three coins to buy straw sandals is the small traveling allowance attached to a plain meal or handed out as a dismissal. Chan masters place it after “eat the customary cakes,” give the three coins to a questioner, and use the line as a compact send-off after an answer has run its course. Yunfeng Wenyue says that if nobody can supply the requested sentence, eating the customary cakes will still earn three coins for straw sandals. Zhenjing Kewen repeats the meal-and-sandals line, then immediately poses another old-case question. Muting Pufu gives the phrase directly to his questioner after that questioner thanks him for instruction. Yuejiang Zhengyin says he differs from Dongshan Shouchu, then caps the contrast with the same customary meal and sandal money.

Senses.Explanation: Collected absorption names a collected or absorbed mode, most often inside a specifying compound. Huineng defines the single-conduct form as carrying one straight mind while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; he explicitly rejects defining it as sitting motionless with thought suppressed. Mazu says the ocean-seal form gathers all things as streams return to the sea, and describes dressing, eating, speaking, responding, and using the senses as occurring within the nature-of-things form. Xuansha Shibei calls the buddhas people's own-reception form and says it is never absent in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. The compounds supply their own qualifications, so the bare headword does not reduce them all to one formula.

Senses.Explanation: Beneath three rafters names the concrete monastic sitting place used as a setting for sustained sitting and scrutiny. Donglin Guzhi warns the assembly not to build an understanding by depending on the place beneath three rafters and before the seven-foot platform. Miyun Yuanwu locates blows, sleep, and sitting there. Senses.Explanation: In one transmitted public case, the contrast separates verbal ease from lived execution. Niaoke Daolin answers Bai Juyi’s objection that even a child can state the rule by saying that an eighty-year-old still cannot carry it out. Four works preserve this same Niaoke Daolin–Bai Juyi exchange rather than four separate uses. Niaoke first gives the plain rule “do no evil; carry out every good.” Bai Juyi calls it childishly easy to say; Daolin answers by opposing that verbal ease to the difficulty of an elder actually doing it.

Fenyang Shanzhao says that one phrase contains the three mysteries and three essentials, with guest and host clearly distinguished; his verse also calls them difficult to distinguish and turns from words to their intended point. The compiler of Eyes of Humans and Devas later enumerates the three mysteries and says that one shout encompasses the paired label. Tianyin Yuanxiu identifies the device with Linji and simultaneous illumination and function. Qiran Chaozhi asks which phrase is the three-mysteries-and-three-essentials phrase and elsewhere tells hearers to remove it together with other Linji-house arrangements. Jie'an Wujin lists it among the devices marking the Linji family.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 。人皆謂溈山五世到師，寂爾無傳。殊不知萬仞門墻，擬登者銀山䥫壁。溈仰宗至此五世。法眼宗法眼宗清涼法眼禪師清涼法眼禪師師諱文益，餘杭魯氏子。祝髮詣開元覺律師受具戒。及覺盛化四明，師往習毗尼，工文章。覺奇之，目為吾門之游、夏也。師以玄機一發，雜務俱捐，振錫南邁，抵福州。初見長慶，無所契悟，與進、修輩擬之湖外。既發，值雨，少憩城西地藏。入堂，見藏坐地爐，問師：此行何之？曰：行脚去。曰：行脚事作麼生？曰：不知。曰：不知最親三人附火。因舉肇論至天地與我同根處藏，又曰：山河大地與自己是同是別？修曰：同。藏竪兩指熟視之，兩箇便起去。雨霽辭行，藏送之，問曰：上座尋常說，三界唯心。乃指庭下石曰：且道此石在心內，在心外？師曰：在心內。曰：行脚人著甚來由，安塊石在心頭耶？師窘無以對，遂放包，俱求決擇。近月餘，呈見解，說道理。藏曰：佛法不是恁麼。曰：某甲到此，辭窮理絕也。藏曰：若論佛法，一切見成。師大悟出世。臨川崇壽一香為藏拈。僧子方者問曰：公久親長慶，乃嗣地藏，何哉？師曰：以不解長慶說萬象之中獨露身故。方舉拂子示之。師曰：撥萬象不撥萬象？方曰：不撥萬象。師曰：獨露身𡁠。方曰：撥萬象。師曰：萬象之中。𡁠方於是悟旨。二僧參次，師指簾，二僧齊去捲。師曰：一得一失。示眾云：盡十方世界，皎皎地無一絲頭。若有一絲頭，即是一絲頭。金陵報恩則初參青

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 古人道。三界唯心。萬法唯識
ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 句一時。頌投子了也。末後頌這僧道。可憐無限弄潮人。這僧敢攙旗奪鼓道。和尚莫㞘沸碗鳴聲。又道喚和尚作一頭驢得麼。此便是弄潮處。這僧做盡伎倆。依前死在投子句中。投子便打。此僧便是畢竟還落潮中死。雪竇出這僧云。忽然活便與掀倒禪床。投子也須倒退三千里。直得百川倒流閙𣽅𣽅。非唯禪床震動。亦乃山川岌崿。天地陡暗。苟或箇箇如此。山僧且打退鼓。諸人向什麼處。安身立命岌崿。80【八〇】舉。僧問趙州。初生孩子。還具六識也無趙州云。急水上打毬子僧復問投子。急水上打毬子。意旨如何子云。念念不停流。此六識。教家立為正本。山河大地。日月星辰。因其所以生。來為先鋒。去為殿後。古人道。三界唯心。萬法唯識。若證佛地。以八識。轉為四智。教家謂之改名不改體。根塵識是三。前塵元不會分別。勝義根能發生識。識能顯色分別。即是第六意識。第七識末那識。能去執持世間一切影事。令人煩惱。不得自由自在。皆是第七識。到第八識。亦謂之阿賴耶識。亦謂之含藏識。含藏一切善惡種子。這僧知教意。故將來問趙州道。初生孩子。還具六識也無。初生孩兒。雖具六識眼能見耳能聞。然未曾分別六塵。好惡長短。是非得失。他恁麼時總不知。學道之人要復如嬰孩。榮辱功名。逆情順境。都動他不得。眼見色與盲等。耳聞聲與聾等。如癡似兀。其心不動。如須彌山。這箇是衲僧家。真實得力處。古人道。衲被蒙頭萬事休。此

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 古人道 assigns the paired formula to an unnamed earlier speaker; Yuanwu Keqin introduces it and comments on the senses and consciousness afterward.

Senses.Explanation: The three realms are mind-only is a received proposition that Chan writers quote and put to work rather than leave as an unexplained doctrinal label. A scripture quoted by Yongming Yanshou pairs it with the myriad things being consciousness-only. Huihong’s Forest Notes narrates Wonhyo’s skull-water realization: Wonhyo first says that when mind arises, phenomena arise, and when mind ceases, the skull is not two; he then explicitly quotes the Tathagata’s statement that the three realms are mind-only. In a raised case, Luohan Guichen repeats Fayan Wenyi’s habitual formula, points to a courtyard stone, and asks whether it is inside or outside mind. Yuanwu Keqin introduces the paired saying as an unnamed old speaker’s words before discussing the senses and consciousness. Across these uses the proposition becomes a test of what a speaker will say about present appearances, not permission to replace the concrete chair, stone, skull, or sensory event with an imported abstraction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 石頭大師曰：竺土大僊心，東西密相付。豈其妄言之耶？予謂曰：子讀其文之誤，所謂密付者，非若醫巫家以其術背人相爾汝也，直使其自悟明為密耳。故長慶巘禪師曰：二十八代祖師皆說傳心，且不說傳語，但破疑情，終不於佛心體上答出話頭。如道明上座見六祖於大庾嶺上，既發悟，則曰：此外更有密意也無？六祖曰：我適所說者，非密意也，一切密意盡在汝邊。非特然也，如釋迦於然燈佛所但得授記而已，如有法可傳，則即付與之矣。阿難亦甞猛省曰：將謂如來惠我三昧，前聖語訓具在，可以鏡心。不然，香嚴聞擊竹聲，望溈山再拜；高亭隔江見德山，即橫趨而去。何以密耳語哉？曹山本寂禪師躭章曰：取正命食者，須具三種墮：一者披毛戴角，二者不斷聲色，三者不受食。時會中有稠布衲問：披毛戴角是什麼墮？答曰：是類墮。進曰：不斷聲色是什麼墮？答曰：是隨墮。進曰：不受食是什麼墮？答曰：是尊貴墮。因又為舉其要曰：食者即是本分事，本分事知有不取，故曰尊貴墮。若執初心知有自己及聖位，故曰類墮。若初心知有己事，回光之時，擯却聲色香味觸法，得寧謐即成功勳。後却不執六塵等事，隨分而昧，任之即礙。所以外道六師是汝之師，彼師所墮，汝亦隨墮，乃可取食。食者即是正命食也。食者亦是却就六根門頭見聞覺知，只是不被佗染污將為墮，且不是同向前均，他本分事尚不取，豈況其餘事耶？曹山凡言墮，謂混不得、類不齊耳。

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 石頭大師曰：竺土大僊心，東西密相付。豈其妄言之耶？予謂曰：子讀其文之誤，所謂密付者，非若醫巫家以其術背人相爾汝也，直使其自悟明為密耳。故長慶巘禪師曰：二十八代祖師皆說傳心，且不說傳語，但破疑情，終不於佛心體上答出話頭。如道明上座見六祖於大庾嶺上，既發悟，則曰：此外更有密意也無？六祖曰：我適所說者，非密意也，一切密意盡在汝邊。非特然也，如釋迦於然燈佛所但得授記而已，如有法可傳，則即付與之矣。阿難亦甞猛省曰：將謂如來惠我三昧，前聖語訓具在，可以鏡心。不然，香嚴聞擊竹聲，望溈山再拜；高亭隔江見德山，即橫趨而去。何以密耳語哉？曹山本寂禪師躭章曰：取正命食者，須具三種墮：一者披毛戴角，二者不斷聲色，三者不受食。時會中有稠布衲問：披毛戴角是什麼墮？答曰：是類墮。進曰：不斷聲色是什麼墮？答曰：是隨墮。進曰：不受食是什麼墮？答曰：是尊貴墮。因又為舉其要曰：食者即是本分事，本分事知有不取，故曰尊貴墮。若執初心知有自己及聖位，故曰類墮。若初心知有己事，回光之時，擯却聲色香味觸法，得寧謐即成功勳。後却不執六塵等事，隨分而昧，任之即礙。所以外道六師是汝之師，彼師所墮，汝亦隨墮，乃可取食。食者即是正命食也。食者亦是却就六根門頭見聞覺知，只是不被佗染污將為墮，且不是同向前均，他本分事尚不取，豈況其餘事耶？曹山凡言墮，謂混不得、類不齊耳。

Senses.Explanation: Xuansha's three patients are one blind person, one deaf person, and one person unable to speak, presented in a challenge about how a teacher receives people. Xuansha Shibei says that the blind patient cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, the deaf patient cannot hear spoken instruction, and the mute patient cannot give the requested reply. Dawei compares the difficulty of meeting them to a case before which even the famed physicians Lu and Bian would fold their hands. Liao'an Qingyu raises the case in which a monk asks Yunmen Wenyan for help with Xuansha's three patients, and Yunmen begins by telling him to bow. In another exchange, an unnamed questioner asks Tiantai Deshao what the three patients are, and Deshao answers, 'You have just asked it.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 舍請上堂，云：「微笑拈花事，分明在目前，等閑能薦得，任運復騰騰。既任運，又騰騰，則無世緣依倚，那討佛法廉纖？撒手懸崖隨步樂，橫拈白棒打青天。」遂卓拄杖，下座。舉前堂隱元首座秉拂上堂，問：「玉趾麒麟朱點額，金毛獅子劍張牙，程途底事俱放過，根源一句問歸家？」師云：「問得最親切。」進云：「堂堂獨露乾坤塞，剎剎明宗宇宙新。」師云：「又不相當。」乃云：「搶旗奪鼓，折角衝鋒，須是宿將登壇纔能捉敗，從上古錐世尊拈花，迦葉微笑，馬祖一喝，百丈耳聾，黃檗三頓棒，臨濟無多子，皆遭按下，等閒施一機透過千差，尋常發一語胸襟流出，皆因踏著佛祖上頭關，與教外別傳、單提直指深相符契，故能掀天關、翻地軸，開發西來命脈，展托衲僧巴鼻，掌握從上綱宗，維持叢林統紀，誠為人天眼目炤明于世。凡我會中英靈衲子、俊俏禪和，多負沖天意氣，常佩肘後玄符，正好吹拍相隨，同緣唱和，直令教外別傳臨濟正宗永遠垂芳，纔是報佛報祖之恩，亦為成己成人之德。秪如今日人天交接一句作麼生道？獅子窟中獅子吼，旃檀林裏現旃檀。」下座。禮大悲懺，請

Occurrences.Kwic: 秋。漆桶不快，騎牛覔牛。泝流逢源，洗脚上船。溟鵬九萬，遼鶴三千。老僧口角無憑據，試問通人是非是。是也山環九斗城，非兮江抱龍翔寺。振錫參方宜自決，負吾負汝俱休說。百鍊剛為繞指柔，何似紅爐一點雪。送裕侍者省師送裕侍者省師莧菜根頭足生意，折脚鐺兒提挈去，迢迢自不涉程途，綽綽誰知有餘裕？有呼有應今古同，手面推倒須彌峯，塵毛剎海露迥迥，談笑便可󳭪吾宗。師勝資強水傳器，釋尊不受然燈記，沒蹤跡處解相逢，萬法豈能為伴侶？送明書記送明書記萬仞崖頭轉身句，金毛師子自不類。一吸西江徹底枯，馬師縮首龐公畏。忽然平地波濤翻，浸爛鼻孔何時乾。虗空失笑萬象舞，栴檀葉底香曼曼。拈却洞山三頓棒，凜凜英風爭近傍。北往南來總未知，蕭洲水落沙痕漲。送慶雲東歸積善送慶雲東歸積善海上日出雲之東，天南地北光曈曨。六龍夾飛黃道正，幽岩䆳谷皆春風。少林一花開五葉，竺國支那沒交涉。沒交涉處忽融通，若聖若凡俱慶愜。一大藏教說不到，半座平分顯圓照。太湖三萬六千頃，月在波心誰不了。誰不了，栴檀林裡栴檀繞。次松月翁韻送育王旭書記次松月翁韻送育王旭書記運斤之手受斤質，二妙相遭眼雙碧。鐵鞭鞭起泐潭龍，驪珠迸散慈明室。辟歷一聲飛上天，三關大啟天不言。捋虎須是分內事，豈惟濟北能風顛。咳唾隨風落珠玉，著渠政用天為屋。曹溪波浪拍天高，天瑞流芳󳭪正續。贈萬壽澤藏主贈萬壽澤藏主一代時

Occurrences.Kwic: 南禪師信之，玉山人，族章氏。童齠深沈，年十一去家，師事定水智鑾。嘗侍鑾行次，見祠廟輒杖擊而往。十九落髮受具，遠游至廬山，依歸宗寶、棲賢諟。逾三秋，渡淮謁三角澄。久之，分座雲峰悅禪師，勉趨石霜。至中道，聞石霜不事事，因寓福嚴。時賢禪師命典記室。賢歸寂，適慈明繼席，師出迎之，悚然。及聞其說法，乃貶剝諸方，盡為邪解，皆師歷參所契證者。遂幡然曰：大丈夫心膂之間，豈可自為疑礙？造室求發藥，明揖坐，師固辭哀懇。明曰：書記參雲門禪，必善其旨。如放洞山三頓棒，是合喫不合喫？云：合喫。曰：吾始疑不堪汝師，今乃可使拜之。復曰：洞山三頓棒即且置，那裏是趙州勘破婆子處？師擬對，明擊其口。師大悟，述偈呈之。留月餘辭去，時年三十五。初住同安，次擢歸宗、黃檗、黃龍，得大法者七十有九人。然在積翠庵所接者，多衲子趨風，相與交武，竭蹙于道。初受請日，三角遣僧來審，師提唱之語有曰：智海無性，因覺妄而成凡；覺妄元虗，即凡心而見佛。便爾休去，將謂同安無折合，隨汝顛倒所欲，南斗七，北斗八。僧歸舉似澄，澄不懌。俄聞開堂

Senses.Explanation: To press an ox’s head down to make it eat grass pictures forcing compliance. Liangting Jingting says Juefan Huihong’s deliberate arrangement of the three mysteries onto Xuansha is also this act (覺範特地差排，也是), and points to a detailed refutation. Xueqiao Yuanxin says another person cannot be led by the hand (把手牽他行不得): only that person’s own assent makes it intimate (惟人自肯乃方親), so forcing the ox’s head absolutely cannot be done (决使不得). In the sole retained lamp recension, Youyun Zongmou answers a question about how many people he had received by saying that this mountain monk has never done it (山僧從來不曾). Across these passages the image criticizes imposed explanation or guidance; it is not an agricultural instruction or a prescribed method.

Senses.Explanation: In public interviews it rejects a proposed connection between Cuifeng Chongxian's words and the matter asked about: after an unnamed monk identifies Cuifeng Chongxian with an earlier house, the answer is "what connection does that have?" (有什麼交涉). The phrase also appears in prose criticism. The Blue Cliff Record says that treating Mazu's left and right eyes as the sun-face and moon-face has "what connection?" and that such readers have missed the old matter. Elsewhere Juehua Puzhao asks, "if lips, voice, and appearances are taken as oneself, what connection does that have?" (若以唇吻聲色以為自己，有什麼交涉). In another exchange, an unnamed monk himself uses the question after the answer "the graph 'by means of'" (以字), and receives "the graph 'eight'" (八字), a spoken play on similar-sounding graph names. Zen bends an ordinary request for relevance into a compact interview verdict: the reply or explanation offered has not connected with the exchange.

Senses.Explanation: Do not stay where there is a buddha; hurry past where there is no buddha is a two-sided travel command that removes both stopping places. Masters quote it at departures, retreat endings, and interviews, then ask where anyone could settle after obeying both halves. Jian Xin gives the command to Stonehouse and rejects it as a dead saying until Stonehouse answers. Changshui and Tian'an speak it from the high seat, an unnamed monk asks where to establish a life after it, Hongzhi raises Zhaozhou's wording, and Baochizong sends the assembly onward with it.

Senses.Explanation: Having a phrase and having no phrase names both sides of a single test, most famously the vine leaning on a tree. Yuanwu Keqin recalls Wuzu Fayan pressing him with the formula until his explanations failed; Wuzu is therefore the quoted utterer, not Yuanwu. Dahui Zonggao directly tests whether a listener has penetrated the same saying. Hanyue Fazang and the retained Yangqi lamp preserve further distinct uses.

Senses.Explanation: The paired proverb praises freedom that intensifies existing vigor and produces grace where ordinary elegance is absent. Both sermons use it after urging practitioners beyond habitual constraints. One ordination sermon links it to renewed resolve; a letter to a layman applies it after stripping away emotional and conceptual entanglement.

Senses.Explanation: At times both person and environment are taken away names one selection in Linji's fourfold teaching frame. The retained quotation gives the full sequence: take away the person but not the environment; take away the environment but not the person; take away both; and take away neither. The headword is therefore interpreted inside that four-part contrast rather than as an isolated slogan.

Senses.Explanation: What has that to do with it? is a spoken Chan rejection of a proposed connection. The records place the question after a quotation, classification, or offered formulation and use it to deny that the proposal reaches the matter under examination. Sanshan Denglai rejects both commentary on an old exchange and inert long-bench sitting with the same question. Baiyu Jingsi dismisses a polished account of mind and teaching before setting his staff against it. Yuan'an Liao uses the question twice against stock answers offered for the study-eye and the grounded statement. Hengchuan Rugong applies it first to verbal presentation itself and later to the old moon-viewing exchange, where the masters' displayed answers are said to have nothing to do with the moon.

Senses.Explanation: 有頭無尾 means having a beginning but no completion. The literal head-and-tail contrast remains active: in a case raised by Weilin Daopei, Sushan Kuangren asks first about the head, then the tail, then having a head without a tail, and finally about head and tail matching. Zhe'an Jingfan likewise contrasts someone with a head but no tail against someone with a tail but no head and asks how beginning and ending can correspond. Yangshan Huiji expands the phrase as 有始無終, ‘having a beginning but no ending,’ when predicting Puhua's help for Linji Yixuan. Xuedou Chongxian applies it as a verdict on two case figures whose handling did not carry through. Across these uses it marks incompletion, not literal anatomy.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one's eyebrows fall out in these Chan records. Its wording is the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). In the corpus, the phrase is well attested. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 48 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.

Senses.Explanation: The records use intertwined eyebrows for direct, intimate conjunction: two people or a whole assembly are brought figuratively brow to brow. Feiyin Tongrong pairs the phrase with having walked hand in hand, while Hanxiu Ruqian applies it to the people gathered at a winter retreat. Huguo Zhizhuan sets speaking as separation and not speaking as intertwined eyebrows; Dahui Zonggao demands the same closeness for an honest examination. Liao'an Qingyu says that he and his assembly remained intertwined at the eyebrows even when he could not converse with them, yet adds that failure to notice it became estrangement. Liangting Jingting describes a layman's wish to live beside him and speak together. The phrase therefore does not by itself establish ordinary communication, mutual recognition, or lasting harmony.

Senses.Explanation: Eyebrows and whiskers fall out is a warning of the consequence of mishandling a case. The Raising Old Cases compilation narrates that the temple superintendent’s eyebrows and whiskers fell out after he rebuked Danxia Tianran for burning a wooden buddha. Zhenjing Kewen actively reworks that consequence: if one forms an intention, they fall out; if one does not, he asks what then.

Senses.Explanation: To raise and proclaim is to take up a matter and give it voice. Dao Kai's temple regulations list 隨意舉唱 (freely raise and proclaim) among the activities after tea, and Yuanwu Keqin writes of 提掇舉唱 (lift up and proclaim) in an instruction. Tian'an Sheng's recorded sayings and an early lamp record both preserve an unnamed questioner's question, 如何舉唱 (how should one raise and proclaim?), to a teacher. The term therefore covers active public articulation; it does not itself identify a fixed doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: “Raise a finger” names a visible gesture. Yuanwu Keqin lists finger-raising among public acts that display the house style; Huihong narrates a monk raising a finger to draw in the air; Zhaozhou Congshen raises a finger and asks what it should be called; and Jifei Ruyi points to the place where water will appear. A lamp recension preserves Fushan Fayuan listing the gesture beside raising a whisk.

Senses.Explanation: To raise up and make prominent. Chan records make it a public teaching-seat verb: the named speaker proclaims the sect's purport, presents 'this matter' before the assembly, or is asked in an interview to present a cited event. One opening discourse pairs opening the hall with 'proclaiming the teaching of the school'; another records a whisk transmitted with the charge to present this matter before the human and heavenly assembly. A later discourse says that one sentence had already been presented before the listeners entered the gate.

Senses.Explanation: This balanced expression names the ordinary sounds of crows and magpies. Zhongfeng Mingben includes 鴉鳴鵲噪 among immediately present sights and sounds. An unnamed monk quotes the saying that these sounds “all expound great wisdom”; that contextual predicate is not part of the headword’s lexical meaning.
